# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [4]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

Scenario ID: SCN-005
Title: Empty states (first run, empty tab, no search results)
Type: Edge Case
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
When there are no bookmarks at all (brand-new user), the app shows a welcoming
message that points directly to the "Save a link" action, and both tab counts
show 0, rather than a blank screen. When a tab has no items, it shows a short
message ("Nothing left to read — nice." for To read; "Nothing finished yet." for
Finished). When a search or tag filter returns nothing, the list shows "No
bookmarks match your search." rather than empty space.

## Gherkin
Feature: Graceful empty states

  Scenario: Brand-new user with no bookmarks
    Given no bookmarks have been saved
    When the user opens the app
    Then a welcoming message pointing to "Save a link" is shown
    And both tab counts show 0

  Scenario: Save the first bookmark clears the empty state
    Given no bookmarks have been saved
    When the user saves a bookmark
    Then the welcoming message is replaced by the bookmark in the To read tab

  Scenario: Empty tab message
    Given a tab has no bookmarks in its state
    When the user views that tab
    Then a short message for that tab is shown

  Scenario: No search results
    Given a search term or tag filter matches no bookmarks
    Then the list shows "No bookmarks match your search."

## Assumptions
- The first-run message directs the user to the save action.
- Empty-tab and no-results messages are distinct from the first-run message.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-001, SCN-003, SCN-004

Please walk through these three situations:

- For #1, when details can't be fetched, is **letting you type the title and save anyway** the right response (versus blocking the save)?
- For #3, is **quietly disabling Save until the link is valid** good enough, or would you want a visible "that doesn't look like a link" message?

Scenario ID: SCN-006
Title: Prevent duplicate saves and go to the existing bookmark
Type: Edge Case
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
When the user saves a link that is already saved, the app does not create a
second copy. Instead it shows a note ("You've already saved this — here it is…"),
navigates to the existing bookmark — switching to whichever tab it is in
(including Finished) and clearing any active search/tag filter — highlights it
with a brief flash, and opens it ready to edit so the user can add a tag or
change its status. Two links are considered the same when their web addresses
match after: lowercasing the domain only, and ignoring a single trailing "/".
Capitalisation in the path (and the rest of the address) is significant, because
it can identify a genuinely different page.

## Gherkin
Feature: Avoid duplicate bookmarks

  Scenario: Saving an already-saved link
    Given a bookmark with the same web address already exists
    When the user saves that link again
    Then no second copy is created
    And a message explains it is already saved
    And the app navigates to the existing bookmark, switching to its tab if needed
    And the existing bookmark is highlighted and opened for editing

  Scenario: Domain case and trailing slash are ignored
    Given a bookmark "https://github.com/pallets/flask" exists
    When the user saves "https://GitHub.com/pallets/flask/"
    Then it is recognised as the same bookmark

  Scenario: Path capitalisation is significant
    Given a bookmark "https://github.com/pallets/flask" exists
    When the user saves "https://github.com/pallets/Flask"
    Then it is treated as a different page and saved as a new bookmark

## Assumptions
- Sameness rule: lowercase domain, ignore one trailing slash, keep path/query case.
- On duplicate, the existing item is opened in edit mode.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-001, SCN-003, SCN-007

Each saved bookmark has an "Edit" control that opens an inline editor. The user

Scenario ID: SCN-009
Title: Save-time validation and auto-fill failure
Type: Error Case
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
When the entered text is not a valid web link (does not start with http:// or
https://), the Save button stays disabled and, after the user leaves the link
field, a short message explains why ("That doesn't look like a web link — it
should start with http:// or https://"). When the link is valid but its details
cannot be fetched automatically, the app shows a note ("Couldn't fetch details
for this link — type a title yourself, then save."), leaves the title/description
for the user to fill in, and still lets the user save the bookmark. A failed
automatic lookup never prevents saving the link.

## Gherkin
Feature: Robust saving

  Scenario: Invalid link is explained and blocked
    Given the user types text that is not a valid web link
    When the user leaves the link field
    Then a short message explains the link is not valid
    And the Save button remains disabled

  Scenario: Auto-fill failure still allows saving
    Given the user enters a valid link whose details cannot be fetched
    Then a note invites the user to type a title
    And the user can save the bookmark with a manually entered title

## Assumptions
- Validity check: the link must start with http:// or https://.
- Auto-fill is a convenience; its failure never blocks saving.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-001

A couple of final things I want to settle before I suggest moving from exploring to building — these are about how your bookmarks live, and I'll keep it in plain terms.

**1. Keeping your bookmarks over time.** Everything we've tried so far resets if you close the page — that's just the exploration prototype. In the real app, I'd of course **keep your bookmarks saved so they're all still there when you come back later.** I want to check *where* that should be:
- **(a)** Kept on **this one computer/browser** — simplest, private to that machine, but you wouldn't see the same list on your phone or another laptop.
- **(b)** Kept so you can reach the **same bookmarks from any device** you sign in on.

Given you described it as "a web app I open in my browser," just for you, which matches how you'd actually use it?

**2. Removing a bookmark for good.** You wanted "finished" to *not* delete things — that's the Finished tab. But separately, should there also be a way to **permanently delete** a bookmark you saved by mistake or no longer want at all? Or would you rather never delete, only archive?

Once I know these two, I think we've covered the full picture and I can propose we start building.

content.text:
All flows check out. **Open → http://maker:4001/edge-manage.html**

**Sign-in credentials for review:** email **`demo@bookmarks.test`**, password **`demo123`**

**1. Signing in.** You'll first see a **Sign in** screen (this is the step that lets you reach the same collection from any device).
- Try a wrong password first — it says *"That email or password isn't right."*
- Then sign in with the credentials above to reach your bookmarks. (There's a **Sign out** button top-right.)

**2. Archive — hide from your lists but keep it.** You'll notice a new **Archived** tab (it already has 1 item).
- On a **To read** bookmark, click **Archive**. It vanishes from To read, and the **Archived** count goes up.
- Open the **Archived** tab, find it, and click **↩ Restore** — it returns to your normal lists.

**3. Delete — permanent, with confirmation.** On any bookmark, click **Delete**.
- A confirmation appears: *"…will be permanently removed. This can't be undone."* Click **Cancel** — nothing happens. Click **Delete** again, then confirm — it's gone for good.

Three decisions I'd like your read on:
- **Search stays out of the Archived pile** — when you search from To read/Finished, archived items don't show up (they only appear when you're on the Archived tab). Does that match "hidden from my normal lists," or would you rather search find archived items too?
- **Archiving keeps its read-status** — a finished-then-archived bookmark returns to Finished when restored. Sensible?
- The sign-in itself — is a simple **email + password** the right level, or were you picturing something else?

Scenario ID: SCN-011
Title: Archive a bookmark (hide from lists, keep recoverable)
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
Separately from the To read / Finished reading status, a bookmark can be
archived. Archiving hides it from the normal To read and Finished lists and
places it in a dedicated "Archived" view (a third tab showing a count). Archived
bookmarks are recoverable: a "Restore" control returns the bookmark to the
normal lists. Restoring preserves the bookmark's previous reading status (a
finished-then-archived bookmark returns to Finished). Archived bookmarks are
excluded from normal search results (searching from To read/Finished never shows
archived items); they appear only when the Archived tab is selected. Archiving
is not deletion — nothing is lost.

## Gherkin
Feature: Archive bookmarks

  Scenario: Archive hides from normal lists
    Given a bookmark in To read or Finished
    When the user archives it
    Then it no longer appears in the To read or Finished lists
    And it appears in the Archived tab
    And the Archived count increases

  Scenario: Restore returns it with its reading status
    Given an archived bookmark that was Finished before archiving
    When the user restores it
    Then it returns to the Finished list
    And it is removed from the Archived tab

  Scenario: Archived items are excluded from normal search
    Given an archived bookmark matches a search term
    When the user searches from the To read or Finished view
    Then the archived bookmark is not shown
    And it is only found by viewing the Archived tab

## Assumptions
- Archived is a separate dimension from the To read/Finished reading status.
- Reading status is preserved across archive/restore.
- Archived items are out of scope for normal search by design.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-003, SCN-004, SCN-012

    And it is removed from the Archived tab

  Scenario: Archived items are excluded from normal search
    Given an archived bookmark matches a search term
    When the user searches from the To read or Finished view
    Then the archived bookmark is not shown
    And it is only found by viewing the Archived tab

## Assumptions
- Archived is a separate dimension from the To read/Finished reading status.
- Reading status is preserved across archive/restore.
- Archived items are out of scope for normal search by design.

Scenario ID: SCN-013
Title: Personal sign-in and cross-device persistence
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
The bookmark collection belongs to a personal account and is kept centrally so
the user can reach the same collection from any device. On opening the app, the
user signs in with an email and password. Wrong credentials show an error ("That
email or password isn't right.") and do not grant access. After signing in, the
user sees their own bookmarks; all changes (saving, editing, tags, status,
archive, delete) are kept and are present again on the next visit and on other
devices after signing in. A Sign out control returns to the sign-in screen.

## Gherkin
Feature: Personal account and persistence

  Scenario: Wrong credentials are rejected
    Given the sign-in screen is shown
    When the user submits an incorrect email or password
    Then an error message is shown
    And the bookmarks are not revealed

  Scenario: Successful sign-in shows the user's bookmarks
    Given a registered account with saved bookmarks
    When the user signs in with the correct email and password
    Then the user's bookmark collection is shown

  Scenario: Changes persist across sessions and devices
    Given the user makes changes to their bookmarks
    When the user returns later or signs in from another device
    Then the same up-to-date collection is shown

  Scenario: Sign out
    Given the user is signed in
    When the user signs out
    Then the sign-in screen is shown again

## Assumptions
- Sign-in is email + password (simple, sufficient for a personal single user).
- Bookmarks are stored centrally (server-side), not only on one device.
- Each account sees only its own bookmarks.
- Session persists reasonably so the user is not asked to sign in on every action.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [10]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.

We've now explored the whole picture, including the "what happens when" situations, and everything is settled. Here's what we've agreed the app should do — in plain terms:

**Getting in**
- You sign in with an email and password; your bookmarks live in one place so you can reach the same collection from any device.

**Saving**
- Paste a link and its title and description fill in automatically; you can edit them, add tags (typed as chips, reusing tags you've used before), and add your own personal note.
- If a link's details can't be fetched, you can still type a title and save. Junk that isn't a real link can't be saved, and it tells you why.
- If you save something you already have, it doesn't make a duplicate — it takes you to the existing one, ready to edit.

**Finding again (the heart of it)**
- One search box searches titles, descriptions, notes, links and tags, live as you type, across both To read and Finished. Clicking a tag is a quick shortcut.

**Organizing & keeping tidy**
- **To read / Finished** tabs to separate what's left from what's done (nothing deleted).
- **Archive** to hide something from your normal lists but keep it recoverable (and out of normal search).
- **Delete** to remove something for good, with a confirmation.
- Every bookmark is fully editable: web address, title, description, note, tags, and status.

That's **13 settled flows** in total.

**May I now switch from exploring to actually building this app?** Once you say yes, I'll move into development (Phase 2) and design and implement exactly this scope — I won't add or change scope without checking with you.

One heads-up in the interest of honesty: the "reach it from any device" sign-in means I'll build a small central service to hold your account and bookmarks. I'll keep it simple and focused on this scope. Shall I proceed?

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [13]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Design decisions (Cycle 1)

Lightweight record to enable impact analysis and artifact generation in later
cycles. Behaviour basis: approved scenarios SCN-001..SCN-013.

## Architecture

- **Single Node.js service** (`src/server.js`, Express) serving a JSON API and a
  static browser front-end from `public/`. Chosen because the collection must be
  central and reachable from any device (SCN-013); a server with per-account data
  is required. Alternatives dropped: browser-only storage (localStorage/IndexedDB)
  — rejected because it cannot satisfy cross-device access.
- **SQLite via better-sqlite3** for storage (`src/db.js`). Chosen for zero
  external services (no DB server to provision in this environment) while still
  being a real central store. Alternative dropped: an external Postgres/MySQL —
  unnecessary for a single personal user and would need a service not provided.
- **Vanilla JS front-end** (`public/app.js`), no build step. Chosen to keep the
  toolchain minimal and the app easy to run (`npm start`). The live search and
  inline editing are simple enough not to need a framework.

## Key decisions

- **Live search is client-side** over the full collection loaded at sign-in
  (SCN-004). Rationale: instant as-you-type filtering with highlight is the core
  value; a personal collection is small enough to filter in the browser.
  Performance at large scale is tracked as NF-1 (non-functional backlog).
- **Duplicate detection key** (`src/url.js` `normalizeUrl`): lowercase host,
  strip one trailing "/", keep path/query case-sensitive (SCN-006). Enforced both
  in application logic and by a `UNIQUE (user_id, norm_url)` DB constraint.
- **Reading status vs. archive vs. delete are three separate concerns**
  (SCN-003 / SCN-011 / SCN-012): `finished` (boolean) and `archived` (boolean)
  are independent columns; delete removes the row. Archived items are excluded
  from normal search in the client (only shown on the Archived tab).
- **Auto-fill is best-effort** (`src/metadata.js`, `GET /api/metadata`): on any
  failure the endpoint returns `{ok:false}` and the UI still allows manual save
  (SCN-009). Never blocks saving.
- **Auth**: email + password (SCN-013). Passwords hashed with scrypt + per-user
  salt (`src/auth.js`, NF-2). Sessions are random opaque tokens stored in the
  `sessions` table, delivered as an httpOnly `sid` cookie (SameSite=Lax) so
  cookies work in the review environment over HTTP.
- **Account creation**: a `POST /api/register` endpoint plus a "Create an
  account" toggle on the sign-in screen. This is enabling infrastructure for
  SCN-013 (a personal account must be creatable); it introduces no bookmark
  behaviour beyond the approved scenarios. A review account
  (`demo@bookmarks.test` / `demo123`) is seeded on startup.

## Data model (`src/db.js`)

- `users(id, email UNIQUE, password_hash, created_at)`
- `sessions(token PK, user_id, created_at)`
- `bookmarks(id, user_id, url, norm_url, title, description, note, finished,
  archived, created_at, updated_at, UNIQUE(user_id, norm_url))`
- `bookmark_tags(bookmark_id, tag, PK(bookmark_id, tag))`

## Notable implementation notes

- `[hidden] { display:none !important }` in CSS so the `hidden` attribute always
  wins over component classes that set `display` (overlay/tabs/userbar).
- better-sqlite3 under `node:test` can crash at teardown if many DB handles are
  opened/closed; tests use a single shared in-memory DB closed via `t.after`.

# Acceptance

Phase 4. Present the result to the user and obtain acceptance confirmation.

---

## Acceptance procedure

### Presenting the result

Present the implemented software to the client and report that verification
against the approved scenarios' GWT specifications and the internal tests has
passed. Summarise the verification outcome in plain language and provide access
to the implemented software.

For the first cycle, the report covers all approved scenarios. For later cycles,
it covers the changed scenarios and affected existing scenarios.

### Acceptance confirmation

Ask the client to accept the implemented software as a whole on the basis of
the approved behaviour and the verification report. Acceptance completes the
development work for the cycle.

### Handling client requests

Use the requirement scenarios approved during Phase 1 as the baseline. Classify
each request by whether fulfilling it changes that baseline:

- Implementation error: the implementation does not satisfy an approved
  scenario. Return to Phase 2, fix the implementation, repeat verification in
  Phase 3, and request acceptance again. Preserve the approved scenario.
- Requirement change or addition: fulfilling the request requires changing an
  approved scenario or adding a scenario. Record the request for the next cycle
  in context/session-log.md, retaining the current approved scenarios.

Explain the classification using the previously approved behaviour in plain
language. If the client's request is unclear, clarify whether the software fails
to perform that behaviour or the desired behaviour has changed. Keep requirement
exploration within Phase 1 of the cycle that will address the change.

After recording a requirement change or addition, ask for acceptance of the
current software, for example:
"I've recorded that request for the next cycle. The software implements the
behaviour we approved, and its verification is complete. Do you accept this
software and agree to complete this cycle?"

Wait for the client's explicit acceptance. A request recorded for a later cycle
does not itself constitute acceptance of the current software.

---

## Transition to idle

When acceptance confirmation is complete, switch to the idle state. In this
experiment, the trial ends after acceptance of the first cycle. Retain requests
for later cycles in the session log.

---

## Session log

On acceptance completion, record the following in the session log:
- List of accepted scenarios
- Cycle number
- Acceptance result (approved / partially approved / rejected)
- Requirement changes or additions recorded for a later cycle

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 2]
- Current step: [Development]
- Approved scenarios: [13]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 3]
- Current step: [Verification]
- Approved scenarios: [13]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

The app is built, verified, and ready for you to try.

## Your bookmark app is ready to review

**Open → http://maker:4000**
**Sign in:** email **`demo@bookmarks.test`**, password **`demo123`** — or click **"Create an account"** to make your own (your real personal account, reachable from any device).

### What it does — exactly the 13 flows we agreed
- **Sign in** to your own central collection; **sign out** top-right; your bookmarks persist between visits and across devices.
- **Save a link** — details fill in automatically (from the real page), editable; add **tags** as chips with one-click reuse, and a **personal note**.
- If a page's details can't be fetched, you can **still type a title and save**; an invalid link is explained and blocked.
- Saving a link you already have **doesn't duplicate** — it takes you to the existing one, opened for editing.
- **Live search** as you type across titles, descriptions, notes, links and tags, spanning **To read** and **Finished**; click a tag to filter.
- **To read / Finished** tabs; **Archive** to hide-but-keep (out of normal search, in its own tab, restorable with its status intact); **Delete** for good, with confirmation.
- Every bookmark fully editable: web address, title, description, note, tags, status.

### Verification report (plain language)
I checked the app against every one of the 13 approved behaviours and it passes:
- **9 automated acceptance checks** driving a real browser — sign-in/rejection, saving with auto-fill/tags/note, invalid-link and fetch-failure handling, live search across fields and tabs, tag filtering, finished/archive/restore, duplicate handling, editing with address validation and collision-blocking, delete confirmation, and persistence after sign-out.
- **35 internal tests** covering the link/duplicate rules, metadata parsing, password security, and all data operations with per-account isolation.

All 44 pass. Passwords are stored hashed (never in plain text). A couple of items we agreed were *not* part of this build are noted for later: performance tuning for very large collections, and cross-device sync latency.

**Do you accept this software as meeting the behaviour we approved, completing this first cycle?** If anything doesn't behave as we agreed, tell me and I'll correct it within this cycle; if it's a new idea beyond what we approved, I'll record it for a future cycle.
